obtained.how: a research group's own open copy: the Harkness Laboratory of Fisheries Research (the University of Toronto and Ontario MNR station where the work was based) posts the article PDF in its 'Contributions 2000s' list on harkness.ca

bibliography.checked_against: Crossref and the article's first page
bibliography.note: Can. J. Fish. Aquat. Sci. 58: 342–351 (2001). The page footer gives the DOI as 10.1139/cjfas-58-2-342; Crossref's DOI 10.1139/f00-247 is the same article.

claims.claim: small Ontario lakes with smallmouth held 2.3 fewer small-bodied species
claims.location: p. 345 (PDF p. 4), Results; repeated p. 347 (PDF p. 6), Discussion
claims.quote: Lakes with smallmouth bass contained 2.3 fewer small-bodied species, on average,
claims.conditions: summer survey of 14 central-Ontario lakes of ≤ 50 ha (7 with smallmouth, 7 without), mid-July to mid-August 1998, minnow traps plus visual counts, each lake sampled once. Total species richness did not differ (Mann–Whitney U = 22, p = 0.75)
claims.note: An average; total richness was the same, because lakes with bass held more centrarchids.

claims.claim: in 14 small central-Ontario lakes, fathead minnow, pearl dace, Phoxinus and brook stickleback were absent from every lake with smallmouth
claims.quote: were absent from all summer survey lakes containing smallmouth bass
claims.conditions: the same 14-lake summer survey; 'four of the six vulnerable species'
claims.note: The authors add that not every lake without bass held all four species.

claims.claim: pumpkinseed and yellow perch remained in the lakes with smallmouth
claims.source_value: yellow perch and (in the Pumpkinseed row) pumpkinseed both recorded in all seven lakes with smallmouth (and in only 2 and 3 of the seven lakes without)
claims.conditions: presence–absence from combined trap and visual sampling
claims.note: The closing sentence 'Lakes with bass keep the prey that are hard to catch' is the paper's reading. The article separates a small-bodied cyprinid assemblage from a large-bodied centrarchid one, and smallmouth and yellow perch group together in its correspondence analysis (p. 347).

notes: All three uses check. Table 2 also shows golden shiner and brown bullhead in some bass lakes, and blacknose shiner, pearl dace, Phoxinus, brook stickleback and fathead minnow only in lakes without bass. Fathead minnow (p = 0.01), Phoxinus (p = 0.03), brook stickleback (p = 0.08) and blacknose shiner (p = 0.09) were absent or less abundant with bass (p. 345). Vulnerable species were more abundant in complex than simple habitat where bass were present.
